data.text/markdown:
Oracle Audit

Two families of in-silico AMP oracles disagree in sign about which peptides are antimicrobial. Pick one and watch it happen.

Generative antimicrobial-peptide (AMP) design is scored almost entirely by in-silico oracles — published sequence classifiers that return "probability of being an AMP". Nobody wet-labs a million candidates, so the oracle is the benchmark. This notebook audits the benchmark itself. The test is deliberately blunt. Take three cohorts whose labels nobody disputes:
  • real AMPs — 2,000 curated, experimentally validated antimicrobials,
  • shuffled decoys — the same 2,000 peptides with their residues permuted, so amino-acid composition, length and net charge are preserved and only the sequence order is destroyed,
  • curated non-AMPs — 877 peptides annotated as non-antimicrobial.
A usable oracle must rank real AMPs above both. Several widely cited ones do the opposite: they flag 87.5% of composition-matched shuffles and 66.8% of real AMPs. Design pipelines then select tens of thousands of sequences on exactly that signal.
How to read this Everything recomputes live from per-peptide scores — 4,977 peptides x 16 oracles. The dropdown and sliders are the experiment, not decoration. The last panel is the one that matters: it shows how deep into a ranked pool each oracle stays trustworthy.

1. Where the three cohorts land

If the oracle encodes antimicrobial function, the green distribution (real AMPs) sits to the right of the pink one (its own shuffled decoys). If it encodes composition only, the two distributions collapse onto each other — and in the Family-B oracles the shuffles land to the right.

2. The panel that matters: precision vs selection depth

Both families look fine at the top of a ranked list — the published papers report precision@100, and at k=100 almost everything scores 1.00. Real design pipelines do not stop at 100. The curve below screens real AMPs out of a 50/50 pool against their own shuffled decoys: rank the 4,000 peptides by the selected oracle, descending, and plot precision@k. The marker is the depth at which precision first falls below 0.75 — the point past which the oracle is no longer separating function from composition. That depth differs by roughly 6x between the two families, which is the whole audit in one number.

data.text/markdown:
Data provenance

Every number above is recomputed in-browser from per-peptide oracle scores embedded in this notebook (gzip + base64, ~260 kB), so the published build runs with no server and no login.
  • Peptides — 4,977 sequences: 2,000 curated real AMPs, 2,000 composition-preserving shuffles of those same AMPs (residue permutation preserves length, composition and net charge), 877 curated non-AMPs, and the 100 sequences of a real competition submission.
  • Family A oracles (13) — OmegAMP's hard-negative-trained classifiers: the broad classifier, 5 per-species and 7 per-strain heads. Scored probabilities.
  • Family B oracles (3) — amPEPpy, AMPlify (probabilities) and AMPredictor (predicted MIC in uM, lower = more active; thresholded at the MIC cutoff slider, default 16 uM).
  • Derived live — positive rates at the chosen decision rule, precision@k on the 50/50 real-AMP vs shuffled-decoy pool, and k*, the depth at which precision@k first drops below 0.75 (k >= 20 to avoid small-k noise).
Part of Oracle Audit, an OSI Hackathon 2026 submission: a benchmark-validity audit of the in-silico oracles used to evaluate generative AMP design.
